title: 論語 子路第十三
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 13, 〈子路〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 13 of the Analects, 子路 Zǐlù, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Zilu, the bold disciple who opens it by asking about government. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. More than any other book this one is about governing: Zilu, Zhonggong, Zixia, the Duke of Ye and Duke Ding of Lu all ask how it is done, and the answers keep returning to the ruler's own person — set yourself right and others follow without being ordered (13.6, 13.13). Here are the setting right of names, without which words do not fit and nothing can be done (13.3); Fan Chi's request to learn farming, and the Master's answer that he knows less of it than an old farmer (13.4); the three steps for a crowded state — enrich the people, then teach them (13.9); the Duke of Ye's man who testified that his father had made off with a sheep, and the Master's reply that among his own people a father covers for his son and a son for his father (13.18); the gentleman who is easy with others without simply falling in with them (13.23); and two closing sayings on teaching a people before taking it to war (13.29–13.30). Twice in this book Zhu Xi prints two chapters one after the other with no comment between them, so a single card holds both (13.6–7, 13.13–14). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子路問政。
子曰：「
先之，
勞之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zilu asked about government. The Master said: “Go ahead of the people yourself, and labour on their behalf.”
sentences.n: The book is named 子路 from its opening words; Zhu Xi's heading counts thirty chapters (凡三十章), and so does He Yan's (凡卅章). Zilu is Zhong You 仲由. 先之 and 勞之 are each a verb with 之 'them', the people: 先 'first' is used as a verb, 'to go before', and 勞 láo is 'to toil'. Zhu Xi marks 勞 如字, the plain reading 'to toil', not lào 'to encourage, to reward'; modern practice reads láo either way. He quotes Su Shi (蘇氏): in whatever the people are to do, go first in your own person, and it will be done without orders; in whatever their labours, toil at them yourself, and though worked hard they will not resent it. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads 勞之 as 'put them to work': first lead them by virtue (先導之以徳) so that they trust you, and only then make them labour — as the Changes says, employ the people so that they are glad, and they forget their toil.

sentences.t:
請益。
曰：「
無倦。」
sentences.l:
He asked for more.
He said: “Do not weary.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked for something more. The Master said: “Never let up.”
sentences.n: 請益 'asked for an addition', that is, for more. 無 here is the prohibitive 'do not' (= 毋) — Zhu Xi notes that an old text writes 毋 (無古本作毋). 倦 'to weary', as in 12.14 居之無倦 'dwell on it without wearying'. Hu Yin (胡氏), quoted by Zhu Xi: the brave delight in getting things done but cannot keep it up, so the Master told him this. Master Cheng, quoted by Zhu Xi: when Zilu asked for more, the Master said only 'do not weary' and told him nothing further, to make him think deeply. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Zilu thought it too little and asked for more; 'do not weary' means carry out the above without wearying, and it will do.

sentences.t:
仲弓為季氏宰，
問政。
子曰：「
先有司，
赦小過，
舉賢才。」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)
to manage, to be in charge of

sentences.l:
Zhonggong, serving as steward to the Ji house, asked about government.
The Master said: “Put the officers in charge first,
pardon small errors,
raise up the worthy and the able.”
sentences.i: Zhonggong, when he was steward to the Ji family, asked about government. The Master said: “Let your officers take the lead each in his own work, let small slips go, and promote men of worth and ability.”
sentences.n: Zhonggong is Ran Yong 冉雍 (6.1). 為 wéi 'to serve as'; 宰 is the steward who runs a great house. The answer is three verb–object phrases. 有司 'those who have charge', the officers (8.4). 赦 shè 'to pardon'. 賢 and 才 are two kinds of men — Zhu Xi: 賢 are those with virtue, 才 those with ability. Zhu Xi: 有司 are the various posts; the steward oversees them all, but each task must first be put to the officer concerned, and only afterwards its results checked — so he is not worn out himself and everything gets done. 過 is error by mistake (失誤): the large ones, which do harm, must be punished, but if the small are pardoned, punishment does not run to excess and men's hearts are glad; raise and use the worthy and the able, and every post has its man. He quotes Fan Zuyu: without putting the officers first, the lord does his ministers' work; without pardoning small faults, no one below is left whole; without raising worthy talent, the hundred posts fall into neglect — lacking these three one cannot be steward to the Ji, let alone govern the world. He Yan's Wang Su: in government one should first entrust the officers and afterwards hold them to account for their work.

sentences.t:
曰：「
焉知賢才而舉之？」
曰：「
舉爾所知；
爾所不知，
人其舍諸？」
sentences.l:
He said: “How am I to know the worthy and the able and raise them?”
He said: “Raise those you know;
those you do not know —
would others let them go?”
sentences.i: Zhonggong said: “How am I to recognise the men of worth and ability, to promote them?” The Master said: “Promote those you know. Those you do not know — will others let them slip by?”
sentences.n: 焉 yān 'how?' (Zhu Xi: 於䖍反). 爾所知 'what you know': 所 + verb makes a noun phrase, 'those whom you know'. In 人其舍諸, 其 softens the question into 'would…?', and 諸 is the fused 之乎 'them?' — 'would others let them go?' 舍 shě 'to let go, to leave aside' (Zhu Xi: 上聲). Zhu Xi: Zhonggong worried that he had no way to know all the worthy and able men of his day, so the Master told him this. Master Cheng, quoted by Zhu Xi: a man first loves his own kin, and only then loves beyond his own kin; set 'how am I to know the worthy and raise them?' beside 'raise those you know — will others leave aside those you do not?', and one sees how much larger the sage's heart was than Zhonggong's. Push this meaning through, and one mind can make a state flourish and one mind can ruin it: the difference lies only between public and private. He Yan's Kong Anguo: those you do not know, others will raise of themselves; if each raises those he knows, no worthy talent is left out.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
衛君待子而為政，
子將奚先？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “The lord of Wei is waiting for you, Master, to conduct his government;
what will you put first?”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “The lord of Wei is waiting for you to take his government in hand. What will you see to first?”
sentences.n: 衛君 'the lord of Wei', as in 7.14. 待子而為政 'waits for you and (so) conducts government': 而 links the waiting and the governing, and the lord means to hand the Master the work (為 wéi). 子 is 'you, Master', Zilu speaking to Confucius. 奚先 'what first?': the question word 奚 comes before its verb. Zhu Xi: the lord of Wei was Duke Chu, Zhe 輒; this was the tenth year of Duke Ai of Lu, when Confucius had come back from Chu to Wei. He Yan's Bao Xian: Zilu asks, if the Master went to the post, what he would do first.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
必也正名乎！」
sentences.l: The Master said: “If it must be anything, it would be setting names right!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It would have to be putting names right, surely.”
sentences.n: 必也…乎 is the shape of 3.7 and 12.13: 'if it must be something, it would be…'. 正名 'to set names right', verb + object. Zhu Xi: at this time Duke Chu did not treat his father as father but gave his grandfather a father's place in the ancestral rites (不父其父而禰其祖), so names and realities were in a tangle, and Confucius put setting names right first. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: though it was said with the lord of Wei in view, in the way of government this always comes first. He Yan's Ma Rong reads it more broadly: to set right the names of all the hundred affairs (正百事之名).

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
有是哉，
子之迂也！
奚其正？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “So that is it!
How far from the point you are, Master!
Why set them right?”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “Really? You are a long way from the business in hand, Master. What is there to set right?”
sentences.n: 有是哉 'is there this!' — an incredulous 'so it has come to this?'. 子之迂也 is subject + 之 + predicate, made an exclamation: 'you — so roundabout!' 迂 yū is 'roundabout, off the point' — Zhu Xi: far from the facts of the case (逺於事情), meaning it was not the urgent business of the day; He Yan's Bao Xian likewise glosses it 'far' (逺): the Master's words were far from the matter. 奚其正 'why the setting right?' — 其 before the verb turns it into a musing question. Variant: He Yan's text reads 奚其正名 'why set names right?', adding 名.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
野哉，由也！
君子於其所不知，
葢闕如也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “How rustic, Yóu!
The gentleman, as to what he does not know,
as a rule leaves it aside.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “How uncouth you are, Yóu! Where a gentleman does not know, he holds his tongue and leaves the matter open.”
sentences.n: 野哉由也 puts the predicate first for exclamation, then the man addressed: 'rustic — Yóu!' Zhu Xi: 野 is 'boorish' (鄙俗); he rebukes Zilu for not leaving his doubts aside and answering rashly. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 野 is 'not getting through' (不達). 於其所不知 'with regard to what he does not know'. 葢 gài, the edition's form of 蓋, is 'as a rule, presumably'. 闕如 'leave-aside-like': 闕 quē is to leave a blank, to leave aside (as 2.18 多聞闕疑), and 如 turns it into a description of manner. He Yan's Bao Xian: the gentleman leaves blank what he does not know and does not presume; Zilu did not understand the meaning of setting names right and called it far-fetched. The Master's answer runs on past three of Zhu Xi's comments; the quotation is closed here and the following units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
名不正，則言不順；
言不順，則事不成。
sentences.l:
If names are not right, speech does not run smoothly;
if speech does not run smoothly, affairs are not accomplished.
sentences.i: If names are out of true, words will not run straight; and if words do not run straight, nothing can be carried through.
sentences.n: A chain of conditions, each 則 'then' handing its result on as the next condition. 順 'to go with the grain, to run smoothly'. The unquoted continuation of the Master's answer. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: when a name does not fit its reality, speech does not run smoothly; and when speech does not run smoothly, there is nothing to check the reality by, so affairs are not accomplished.

sentences.t:
事不成，則禮樂不興；
禮樂不興，則刑罰不中；
刑罰不中，則民無所措手足。
sentences.i: When nothing is carried through, the rites and music cannot thrive; when the rites and music do not thrive, punishments miss their mark; and when punishments miss their mark, the people are left without a safe place to stand.
sentences.n: The chain goes on, still unquoted. 禮樂 'the rites and music', 樂 yuè (as 11.1). 興 xīng 'to rise, to flourish'. 刑罰 'punishments and penalties', 罰 fá being the lighter. 中 zhòng 'to hit the mark' (Zhu Xi: 去聲): punishments that fit the offence. 無所措手足 'have no place where they may set hand and foot': 所 + verb again makes a noun, 'a place to put', and 措 cuò is 'to place'. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: affairs having their order is what is called the rites, things having their harmony is what is called music; if affairs are not accomplished there is neither order nor harmony, so the rites and music do not flourish, and then everything applied in government loses its way, so punishments miss the mark. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the rites keep those above secure and music changes customs; where these two are not carried out, punishment runs wild and penalties go to excess.

sentences.t:
故君子名之必可言也；
言之必可行也。
君子於其言，
無所苟而已矣。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
So the gentleman, naming a thing, can surely speak of it;
speaking of it, can surely carry it out.
The gentleman, in his speech,
is careless in nothing, and that is all.
sentences.i: So when a gentleman gives a thing a name, it is a name he can put into words, and what he puts into words he can carry out. In what he says, the gentleman leaves nothing to chance; that is the whole of it.
sentences.n: Still unquoted. 名 'a name' is here a verb, 'to name'; 之 'it' is whatever is named. 必可言 'surely can be spoken of' and 必可行 'surely can be done', 行 xíng. 無所苟 'has nothing in which he is careless': 苟 is 'casual, careless'; 而已矣 'and that is all'. He Yan's Wang Su: what he names can surely be stated plainly; what he states can surely be followed and done. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: name and reality depend on each other; if one thing is careless, all the rest are careless too. And Hu Yin tells the story behind the chapter: Kuaikui 蒯聵, heir of Wei, ashamed of his mother Nanzi's lewdness, tried to kill her, failed, and fled. Duke Ling wished to make Prince Ying 郢 his heir, but Ying declined; when the duke died his widow would have set Ying up, and he declined again; so they set up Kuaikui's son Zhe to keep Kuaikui out. Kuaikui had sought to kill his mother and offended his father, and Zhe held the state against his father: both were men without a father, plainly unfit to hold a state. Had the Master governed, putting the setting right of names first, he would have laid the whole matter before the Zhou king, made his request to the regional overlord, and had Prince Ying installed; then the bonds between men would be right and Heaven's principle served — names right, speech running smoothly, affairs accomplished. The Master told Zilu this in full, and Zilu never understood: he served Zhe, did not leave, and in the end died in the troubles, knowing only that it is right not to flee the troubles of the man whose food one eats, not that eating Zhe's food was itself not right.

sentences.t:
樊遲請學稼。
子曰：「
吾不如老農。」
請學為圃。
曰：「
吾不如老圃。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l:
Fan Chi asked to learn grain-growing.
The Master said: “I am no match for an old farmer.”
He asked to learn gardening.
He said: “I am no match for an old gardener.”
sentences.i: Fan Chi asked if he might learn to grow grain. The Master said: “Any old farmer knows more of that than I do.” He asked if he might learn to raise vegetables. “Any old gardener knows more of that than I do.”
sentences.n: Fan Chi is Fan Xu 樊須 (2.5), whom the Master names in the next unit. 稼 jià is sowing grain and 圃 pǔ a plot for greens — Zhu Xi: sowing the five grains is called 稼, sowing vegetables 圃; He Yan's Ma Rong says the same with 樹 'to plant'. 為圃 'to do (the work of) the vegetable plot', 為 wéi; in 老圃 the same word stands for the man who works it. 不如 'not equal to'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子曰吾不如老圃, adding 子 to the second reply.

sentences.t:
樊遲出。
子曰：「
小人哉，
樊須也！」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲
a small man — one of the humble folk
Fan Xu — Fan Chi's personal name

sentences.l:
Fan Chi went out.
The Master said: “A small man,
Fan Xu!”
sentences.i: When Fan Chi had gone out, the Master said: “Fan Xu's sights are those of a humble labourer!”
sentences.n: 小人哉樊須也 puts the verdict first for exclamation, then the man: 'a small man — Fan Xu!' The Master uses his personal name, Xu 須. Zhu Xi: 小人 here means the humble folk (細民), those whose work Mencius calls 'the business of small men' — the people who labour with their hands, as against the great men who govern — not the petty man set against the gentleman. The Master's speech runs on after Zhu Xi's comment; the continuation is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
上好禮，則民莫敢不敬；
上好義，則民莫敢不服；
上好信，則民莫敢不用情。
夫如是，則四方之民襁負其子而至矣，
焉用稼？
sentences.i: Let those above love the rites, and not one of the people will dare be disrespectful; let them love what is right, and not one will dare hold out against them; let them love good faith, and not one will dare hide what he truly feels. Where things are so, people from every quarter will come, their infants slung on their backs. Why would anyone need to grow grain?
sentences.n: Three matched conditions: 上 'those above' is the subject of 好 hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 莫敢不 'none dares not', a double negative making a strong positive. 服 'to submit, to be won over'. 用情 'to bring out their true feelings': Zhu Xi glosses 情 qíng as 'sincerity, the plain truth' (誠實), and Kong Anguo in He Yan as 'the real state' (情實) — the people, changed by those above, each answer with what they truly are. 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶) opens the conclusion. 四方 'the four quarters', every direction, so the states round about. 襁 qiǎng is a sling for a baby — Zhu Xi: woven of cords, to tie a small child to the back; he spells it 居丈反 (jiǎng), and modern usage reads qiǎng. 焉 yān 'what?' (於䖍反). Zhu Xi: the rites, what is right and good faith are the business of great men; love what is right and affairs fit as they should; reverence, submission and true feeling each answer to their kind. He quotes Yang Shi: Fan Chi studied at the sage's gate and asked about farming and gardening — a mean aim. Why not refuse him outright, rather than wait till he had gone to say what was wrong? When he asked, the Master said he was no match for a farmer or a gardener, and that was rebuff enough; but Xu's understanding did not reach that far and he could not ask further, could not 'come back with the other three corners' (7.8), so the Master said no more. Once he had gone, the Master feared he would never understand and would go and learn from old farmers and gardeners, straying further still; so he spoke again, to let him know the earlier words had a point. He Yan's Bao Xian: the rites, what is right and good faith are enough to make virtue whole — what use is learning farming to teach the people? and 'carrying in a device' is 襁.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
誦詩三百；
授之以政，不達；
使於四方，不能專對：
雖多，
亦奚以為？」

morph.gloss: a region, a quarter, a direction

sentences.i: The Master said: “A man may chant the Odes through, every one of the three hundred; but if he is handed a task of government and cannot see it through, or is sent abroad and cannot answer for himself, then for all he has learned, what good is it to him?”
sentences.n: Three short conditions, each 'if…, then not'. 誦 'to recite, to chant'; 詩三百 'the Odes, three hundred', as 2.2. 授之以政 'hand him government': 之 is the man, 以 marks what is handed. 達 'to get through, to carry it off' — Zhu Xi: one who recites the Odes ought to have mastered government (達於政). 使 'to be sent on a mission': Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (shì), a reading modern practice does not keep. 四方 'the four quarters', the other states. 專對 'to answer singly': 專 zhuān is 'alone, on one's own' (Zhu Xi and He Yan: 獨也) — an envoy had to reply to his hosts himself, without sending home for instructions. 雖多 'though (it is) much'; 亦奚以為 'what is it used for, then?' — 以 'to use', 為 wéi closing the question. Zhu Xi: the Odes are rooted in human feeling and take in the principles of things; through them one can test the rise and fall of customs and see where government succeeds or fails, and their words, warm, mild and even, are good at indirect admonition — so whoever recites them must be able to govern and to speak. He quotes Master Cheng: one studies the classics to put them to use; can the reciters of the Odes in our day actually govern and answer as envoys? If not, what they have learned is the mere tail-end of chapter and verse — the great bane of scholars. Variant: He Yan's text reads 亦奚以為哉, with a final 哉.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
其身正，
不令而行；
其身不正，
雖令不従。」
子曰：「
魯衛之政，
兄弟也。」

morph.gloss: deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “His own person upright,
without orders, things are done;
his own person not upright,
though he orders, he is not followed.”
The Master said: “The governments of Lu and Wei —
brothers.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a ruler is upright himself, things get done though he gives no orders; if he is not, his orders will go unheeded.” The Master said: “In their government, Lu and Wei are a pair of brothers still.”
sentences.n: This card holds two chapters, 13.6 and 13.7, which the edition prints with only a ○ between them and no commentary on the first; Zhu Xi's comment follows the second. 13.6: two matched halves on 其身 'his own person', the ruler's. 不令而行 'not ordering, and (it) goes': 令 'to command' (the note in He Yan: 令 is 教令 'instructions'), 行 xíng 'to go forward, to get done'. 雖令不従 'though he orders, (they) do not follow': 従 cóng is the edition's form of 從. Compare 12.17 政者正也. 13.7: 魯衛之政 'the governments of Lu and Wei'; 兄弟也 '(are) brothers'. Zhu Xi: Lu descended from the Duke of Zhou and Wei from Kangshu, his younger brother, so they were brother states from the start; at this time both had sunk into decline and disorder, and their governments were alike too, so Confucius sighed over them. He Yan's Bao Xian says nothing of decline: Lu was the Duke of Zhou's fief and Wei Kangshu's; the two founders were brothers and Kangshu was close to the Duke of Zhou, so the governments of their states were like brothers too.

sentences.t:
子謂衛公子荆：「
善居室。
始有，曰：『苟合矣。』
少有，曰：『苟完矣。』
富有，曰：『苟美矣。』」

morph.gloss: Prince Jing — a grandee of Wei

sentences.l:
The Master said of Prince Jing of Wei: “He was good at keeping house.
When he first had things, he said: ‘More or less it comes together.’
When he had a little more, he said: ‘More or less it is complete.’
When he had plenty, he said: ‘More or less it is fine.’”
sentences.i: The Master said of Prince Jing of Wei: “He knew how to live in a house. When he first came to own a little, he said: ‘This will about serve.’ When he had a little more: ‘This is about all one could need.’ When he grew rich: ‘This is about as handsome as need be.’”
sentences.n: 子謂 'the Master said of'. 公子荆 'Prince Jing', a son of a ruling house; Zhu Xi calls him a grandee of Wei, and He Yan's Wang Su counts him with Qu Yuan 蘧瑗 and Shi Qiu 史鰌 among the gentlemen of Wei. 善居室 'good at dwelling in a house' — at managing his household and its goods. Three matched steps: 始有 'when he first had (something)', 少有 'when he had a little (more)' (少 shǎo), 富有 'when he had plenty'. In each saying 苟 is 'roughly, more or less' — Zhu Xi: makeshift and rough (聊且粗畧之意); 合 hé is 'gathered' (聚也), 完 wán 'fully provided' (備也). Zhu Xi: he went on in due order and with measure, and did not burden his heart with haste to have everything fine. He quotes Yang Shi: work at making everything whole and fine, and one is burdened by things and a proud, grasping heart is born; Prince Jing said 'more or less' each time, not setting his heart on outward things, because his wants were easily met.

sentences.t:
子適衛，
冉有僕。

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l:
The Master went to Wei;
Ran You drove.
sentences.i: When the Master went to Wei, Ran You was at the reins.
sentences.n: 適 shì 'to go to'. Ran You is the disciple Ran Qiu 冉求. 僕 pú is 'a servant', here a verb, 'to drive (the carriage)' — Zhu Xi: 御車也; He Yan's Kong Anguo: when Confucius went to Wei, Ran You was his driver.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
庶矣哉！」
sentences.l: The Master said: “How numerous!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What a lot of people!”
sentences.n: 庶 shù is 'many, numerous' (Zhu Xi: 衆也); He Yan's Kong Anguo: the people of Wei were many. 矣哉 together make a strong exclamation: 'numerous indeed!'

sentences.t:
冉有曰：「
既庶矣，
又何加焉？」
曰：「
富之。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l:
Ran You said: “Once they are numerous,
what further is to be added?”
He said: “Make them rich.”
sentences.i: Ran You said: “They are many already; what is to be added to that?” “Make them prosperous.”
sentences.n: 既…矣 'once (it is) already…'. 又何加焉 'further, what to add to it?' — 焉 'to it' (= 於之). 富之 'enrich them': the adjective 富 'rich' used as a causative verb, 'make them rich'. Zhu Xi: numerous but not rich, the people's livelihood does not prosper; so lay out fields and homesteads and lighten the taxes, to make them rich.

sentences.t:
曰：「
既富矣，
又何加焉？」
曰：「
教之。」
sentences.l:
He said: “Once they are rich,
what further is to be added?”
He said: “Teach them.”
sentences.i: “And when they are prosperous, what then?” “Teach them.”
sentences.n: The same frame again. 教 jiào 'to teach'. Zhu Xi: rich but untaught, they come close to birds and beasts; so set up schools and make plain the rites and what is right, to teach them. He quotes Hu Yin: Heaven gave birth to the people and set over them shepherds charged with these three tasks, but since the Three Dynasties hardly one or two rulers in a hundred have done the work. Han Wendi and Mingdi and Tang Taizong may be said to have made their people numerous and rich; of teaching under the Western Han nothing is heard, while Mingdi honoured his teachers and Taizong summoned famous scholars and enlarged the schools — teaching enough, yet they did not know what teaching is, for in the Three Dynasties the Son of Heaven and his ministers practised it in their own persons, so that all their words, deeds and government could serve as a model. Could those rulers do that?

sentences.t:
子曰：「
苟有用我者，
期月而已，可也；
三年有成。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Were anyone to put me to use, within a single year things would be in passable order, and in three years the work would be done.”
sentences.n: 苟 'if'; 有用我者 'there is one who employs me' — 者 makes the phrase 'one who…'. 期 jī is a full round of time: Zhu Xi says 期月 means the months of one full turn of the year (周一嵗之月), a whole year. 而已 'and no more'. 可 'it would do' — Zhu Xi calls it a word of bare sufficiency (僅辭): the main lines of order would be laid down. 有成 'there would be accomplishment', the work of government complete. He quotes Yin Tun: Confucius lamented that no one in his day could use him; and adds his own note: by the Shiji, this was said when Duke Ling of Wei would not employ him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: if someone truly used me in the business of government, in a full year I could put my government and teaching into effect, and in three years it would be complete.

sentences.t:
子曰：「『
善人為邦百年，
亦可以勝殘去殺矣。』
誠哉是言也！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “‘Good men governing a state for a hundred years
could indeed master cruelty and put an end to killing.’
True, how true, this saying!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “‘Give a state to good men for a hundred years, and they could tame the violent and have no more need of executions.’ That saying is right!”
sentences.n: The Master quotes an old saying and then approves it — Zhu Xi: there was this saying of old and the Master praised it; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same. 善人 'a good man', ranked below the sage (as in Books 7 and 11). 為邦 'to run a state', 為 wéi; 百年 'a hundred years' — Zhu Xi: one succeeding another over a long time. 勝殘去殺 'master the cruel and put an end to killing': Zhu Xi reads 勝 平聲 (shēng) and 去 上聲 (qǔ); modern usage reads shèng and qù, and so do we. He explains 勝殘 as transforming cruel and violent men so that they do no evil, and 去殺 as the people being so changed toward good that executions are no longer needed; He Yan's Wang Su says the same. 殘 cán 'cruel, violent'; 殺 shā 'to kill'. 誠哉是言也 puts the predicate first: 'true — how — this saying!' Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: from Gaozu and Hui down to Wen and Jing, the Han's common people grew simple and honest and punishments were all but laid aside — that came near it; and Yin Tun: mastering cruelty and putting an end to killing is only to stop men doing evil; such is the good man's achievement, but a sage would not need a hundred years, nor would his transforming stop there.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
如有王者，
必世而後仁。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If there were a true king,
it must take a generation, and only then humaneness.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Even under a true king, humaneness would need a generation to take hold.”
sentences.n: 如有 'if there were'. 王者 'one who is king' — Zhu Xi: a sage who receives Heaven's mandate and rises (聖人受命而興). 世 shì 'a generation', thirty years (Zhu Xi: 三十年為一世; He Yan's Kong Anguo: 三十年曰丗). 而後 'and only after that'. 仁 is humaneness taking hold in the people — Zhu Xi: teaching and transformation have soaked right through (教化浹也). He quotes Master Cheng: the Zhou, from Kings Wen and Wu down to King Cheng, only then saw the rites and music flourish — that is the proof. Asked why three years (13.10) and a generation differ in speed, Master Cheng answered: 'in three years there would be accomplishment' means that laws and order are set and the transforming is under way; to steep the people in humaneness and rub them with what is right until it soaks their flesh and sinks into their bones, so that the rites and music can flourish — that is what 仁 means here, and only long accumulation brings it. Kong Anguo: a king who received the mandate would need thirty years before his humane government was complete.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
苟正其身矣，
於従政乎何有？
不能正其身，
如正人何？」
冉子退朝。
子曰：「
何晏也？」
對曰：「
有政。」
子曰：「
其事也。
如有政，
雖不吾以，
吾其與聞之。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “If one sets one's own person right,
in government, what trouble would one have?
If one cannot set one's own person right,
what of setting others right?”
Master Ran came back from court.
The Master said: “Why so late?”
He replied: “There was government business.”
The Master said: “It was household business, surely.
Had there been government business,
though I am not employed,
I would surely have had a share in hearing of it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Let a man once set himself right, and what would hold him back in government? If he cannot set himself right, what can he do about setting others right?” Master Ran came back from court. The Master said: “Why so late?” He replied: “There was business of state.” The Master said: “That will have been the Ji family's own affairs. Business of state I should have heard of, though no one employs me now.”
sentences.n: This card holds two chapters, 13.13 and 13.14, which the edition prints with only a ○ between them and no commentary on the first; Zhu Xi's comment follows the second. 13.13: 苟 'if'; 正其身 'set one's own person right', the theme of 13.6. 於従政乎何有 is the phrase of 6.6, 'in government, what (difficulty) would he have?' — 従 cóng, the edition's form of 從. 如正人何 'what to do about setting others right?', the frame 如…何 of 3.3 and 4.13. 13.14: 冉子 'Master Ran' is Ran Qiu, then steward to the Ji house. 退朝 'to withdraw from court', 朝 cháo (Zhu Xi: 音潮). 晏 'late' (Zhu Xi: 晚也). 其事也 'it was (mere household) business, surely': 其 marks a confident guess. 不吾以 'do not employ me': in a negated sentence the pronoun object 吾 comes before the verb, and 以 is 'to use' (Zhu Xi: 以，用也). 其與聞之 'would surely have had a share in hearing it', 與 yù 'to take part in' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi: the court here is the Ji family's private court; 政 is the government of the state, 事 the business of a house. By the rites a grandee, even out of office, still has a share in hearing state business. At that time the Ji held Lu in their grip, and on matters of state they did not debate with their peers at the duke's court but plotted alone with their house officers in private; so the Master spoke as if he did not know: this must be the Ji house's own business, for had it been state government, he who had been a grandee would have heard of it, though not employed — and since he had not, it was not state government. His aim, Zhu Xi says, went deep: to set names and stations right, check the Ji, and teach Ran You. He Yan's commentators read it differently: Zhou Shenglie (周生烈) takes 退朝 as coming back from the court of the lord of Lu, and Ma Rong takes 政 as some change or reform (有所改更匡正) and 事 as the ordinary business of every day: had there been anything out of the ordinary, he, a grandee, though not given office, would surely have heard of it.

sentences.t:
定公問：「
一言而可以興邦，有諸？」
孔子對曰：「
言不可以若是其幾也。」

morph.gloss: Ding, posthumous name of Duke Ding of Lu
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Duke Ding asked: “One saying, and by it a state can be made to flourish — is there such a thing?”
Kongzi answered, saying: “A saying cannot be counted on like this for its effect.”
sentences.i: Duke Ding asked: “Could a state be made to flourish by one saying alone — is there any such thing?” Kongzi answered: “No saying can be relied on to work as surely as that.”
sentences.n: 定公 is Duke Ding of Lu (3.19), whose personal name was Song. 一言而可以興邦 'one saying, and by it one can make a state flourish': 興 xīng 'to rise' is here transitive, 'to raise up', with 邦 as its object. 有諸 'is there (such a thing)?' — 諸 is the fused 之乎. 孔子對 'Kongzi answered': the book names him Kongzi when he answers a ruler. 言不可以若是其幾也: 若是 'like this'; 幾 jī is the hard word. Zhu Xi glosses it 期 'to look for, to expect (a result)', citing the Ode line 如幾如式, and explains: within the span of one saying, one cannot in this way count for certain on its effect (言一言之間未可以如此而必期其效). He Yan's Wang Su takes 幾 as 近 'near': no single saying, by its gist, can set a state up; but there are sayings that come near to it. Kongzi's answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comments; the next two units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
人之言曰：「
為君難；
為臣不易。」
sentences.i: There is a common saying: “A ruler's lot is hard, and a minister's is no easier.”
sentences.n: Kongzi's answer continues, unquoted; the saying he cites is quoted. 人之言 'people's words', what people say. 為 wéi 'to be, act as'. 難 nán 'hard'. 易 is yì 'easy' — Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, the reading for 'easy' as against 'to change'; modern Mandarin reads both yì. Zhu Xi: there was such a saying at the time (當時有此言也).

sentences.t:
如知為君之難也，
不幾乎：一言而興邦乎？
sentences.l:
If one knows the hardness of being lord,
is it not to be looked for: one saying, and a state made to flourish?
sentences.i: If a ruler truly understood how hard it is to rule, could he not count on that one saying to make his state flourish?
sentences.n: Still Kongzi, unquoted. 為君之難 'the hardness of being lord': 之 joins the phrase 為君 to 難 as 'of'. 不幾乎…乎 is a question expecting 'yes'. Zhu Xi keeps his reading 期 'to look for': having learned from this saying how hard it is to be lord, a ruler will be 'trembling and wary, as at the edge of a deep pool, as treading thin ice' (戰戰兢兢臨深履薄, the Ode of 8.3), and dare neglect nothing — then can this saying not surely be looked to to make the state flourish? He adds that Kongzi was speaking to Duke Ding, so he left out the minister's half. He Yan's Wang Su takes 幾 here too as 'near, nearly': 'is it not close to one saying making a state flourish?' Kong Anguo (in He Yan): a thing cannot be done by one saying, but knowing this, one can come near it.

sentences.t:
曰：「
一言而喪邦，有諸？」
孔子對曰：「
言不可以若是其幾也。
人之言曰：『
予無樂乎為君，
唯其言而莫予違也。』」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Duke said: “One saying, and by it a state is lost — is there such a thing?”
Kongzi answered, saying: “A saying cannot be counted on like this for its effect.
People's saying goes:
‘I have no joy in being lord,
only in this: my words — and no one goes against me.’”
sentences.i: “And could one saying alone lose a state?” Kongzi answered: “No saying can be relied on to work as surely as that. But there is a common saying: ‘Being a ruler gives me no pleasure, except that whatever I say, nobody contradicts me.’”
sentences.n: 喪 is sàng 'to lose' (Zhu Xi: 去聲, and so below). 予 yú 'I, me'. 樂 lè 'joy' (Zhu Xi: 音洛). 無樂乎為君 'have no joy in being lord': 乎 here is 'in' (= 於). 唯其言而莫予違 'only (this): my words, and no one goes against me' — 其 'his', the speaker's own; 莫予違 is 莫違予 with the pronoun object 予 drawn before the verb, as an object pronoun is after a negative like 莫. Zhu Xi: it means he takes joy in nothing else, only in this (言他無所樂，惟樂此耳). Variants: He Yan's text reads 一言而可䘮邦有諸 (䘮 its form of 喪), adding 可 'can', as in the Duke's first question, and 唯其言而樂莫予違也, adding 樂: 'only in my words do I take joy, that no one goes against me' — Kong Anguo explains it so (所樂者唯樂其言而不見違也).

sentences.t:
如其善而莫之違也，
不亦善乎？
如不善而莫之違也，
不幾乎：一言而喪邦乎？
sentences.l:
If his words are good and no one goes against them,
is that not good indeed?
If they are not good and no one goes against them,
is it not to be looked for: one saying, and a state lost?
sentences.i: If what he says is good and nobody contradicts it, well and good. But if what he says is not good and still nobody contradicts it — could one not count on that one saying to lose him his state?
sentences.n: Kongzi's answer continues, unquoted. 莫之違 'no one goes against them': again the object pronoun 之 stands before the verb after 莫. 不亦…乎 'is it not indeed…?' (1.1). The last line answers unit 27 word for word, with 喪 sàng for 興. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: if his words are not good and no one goes against them, wholehearted words never reach his ears; the lord grows prouder by the day and his ministers more fawning, and no such state has ever failed to be lost. And Xie Liangzuo: knowing how hard it is to be lord, a ruler will hold himself with reverent care; wanting only that no one go against his words, he draws slanderers and flatterers to him; the state need not rise or fall at once, but the springs of rising and falling part here — and only a gentleman who sees the first small signs could know it. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): if what the ruler says is good and none goes against it, that is good; if it is not good and none dares go against it, then one saying comes near to losing the state.

sentences.t: 葉公問政。

morph.gloss: Ye: a town of Chu (葉公 'the Duke of Ye')

sentences.l: The Duke of Ye asked about government.
sentences.i: The Duke of Ye asked about governing.
sentences.n: 葉公 the Duke of Ye is Shen Zhuliang 沈諸梁, governor of the county of Ye in Chu, who took the title of duke for himself (7.18). Zhu Xi notes only that the sound and sense are given in Book 7 (音義並見第七篇), where he reads 葉 shè; standard Mandarin reads yè, which we give.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
近者説，
逺者來。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The near ones pleased,
the far ones coming.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When those close by are content, those far off come to you.”
sentences.n: Two clauses of the same shape, each a 者 phrase and a verb: 近者 'those near', 逺者 'those far' (逺 is the edition's form of 遠 yuǎn). 説 is yuè 'pleased' (Zhu Xi: 音悦), the word later written 悅, as in 1.1 不亦説乎. Zhu Xi: those who receive his bounty are pleased, those who hear of his ways come; but only when those near are pleased will those far off come.

sentences.t:
子夏為莒父宰，
問政。
子曰：「
無欲速，
無見小利。
欲速，則不達；
見小利，則大事不成。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: When Zixia was steward of Jufu he asked about governing. The Master said: “Do not try to hurry things, and do not keep looking for petty advantage. Hurry, and you will never get there; look for petty advantage, and nothing great will ever be finished.”
sentences.n: 子夏 Zixia is the disciple Bu Shang 卜商 (1.7). 莒父 Jufu was a town of Lu (Zhu Xi: 魯邑名; Zheng Xuan in He Yan: by the old account, a lesser town of Lu); 父 is read fǔ, as in place names (Zhu Xi: 音甫). 宰 'steward', the governor of a town. 無 'do not' forbids (He Yan's text writes 毋). 見 jiàn 'to see', here 'to fix one's eye on'. 欲速則不達: each of the last two lines is a condition and its result, joined by 則 'then'. Zhu Xi: wanting things done quickly, one is hurried and without order, and fails to get through; seeing the profit in small things, what one achieves is small and what one loses great. He quotes Master Cheng: when Zizhang asked about government he was told 'dwell on it without wearying, carry it out with wholeheartedness' (12.14); when Zixia asked, this. Zizhang's fault was always to aim too high and fall short of humaneness, Zixia's to stay with the near and the small; so each was told what bore closely on himself. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): affairs cannot be done in haste — want them fast and they do not come off; small gains get in the way of great affairs.

sentences.t:
葉公語孔子曰：「
吾黨有直躬者：
其父攘羊，
而子證之。」

morph.gloss: Ye: a town of Chu (葉公 'the Duke of Ye')
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Duke of Ye told Kongzi, saying: “In our community there is one straight in his person:
his father made off with a sheep,
and the son testified to it.”
sentences.i: The Duke of Ye told Kongzi: “Among our people there is a man who is straight through and through. When his father kept a sheep that had wandered his way, the son came forward and testified to it.”
sentences.n: 語 is yù 'to tell' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 吾黨 'our community', the Duke's own district (黨 as in 5.21 吾黨之小子). 直躬者 'one who is straight in his person' — Zhu Xi: one who goes about with his person straight (直身而行者), the same as Kong Anguo in He Yan; some other early writings tell the story of a man they call 直躬 as if it were his name, but neither commentary takes it so. 攘 rǎng is to steal what chance puts in one's way (Zhu Xi, and Zhou Shengle in He Yan: 有因而盜曰攘), as when a stray animal comes into one's hands. 證 zhèng 'to give evidence, testify'. 子 here is 'the son', not 'the Master'; 而 sets the son's act against the father's.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
吾黨之直者異於是：
父為子隠，
子為父隠。
直在其中矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said: “The straight ones of our community differ from this:
the father keeps it hidden for the son,
the son keeps it hidden for the father.
Straightness lies in the midst of it.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “The straight men among my people are different. A father keeps quiet about what his son has done, and a son about what his father has done; and that is just where straightness is.”
sentences.n: 為 is wèi 'for, on behalf of' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 隠 (the edition's form of 隱) yǐn 'to hide, keep hidden'. 異於是 'differ from this': 於 marks what is compared. 直在其中矣 'straightness lies in the midst of it', the shape of 7.15 樂亦在其中矣. Zhu Xi: for father and son to hide for each other is the height of Heaven's principle and of human feeling; so they do not seek to be straight, and straightness is there within it. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: to accord with principle is to be straight — would a father who did not hide for his son, or a son for his father, accord with principle? Had the blind old man Gusou killed a man, Shun would have stolen away with him on his back and gone to live by the sea (Mencius's case); at such a time the heart that loves its parent wins out — what leisure is there to reckon straight or not straight? He Yan prints no comment on these lines.

sentences.t:
樊遲問仁。
子曰：「
居處恭；
執事，敬；
與人，忠。
雖之夷狄，
不可棄也。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲
the Yi, the peoples of the east
the Di, the peoples of the north

sentences.i: Fan Chi asked about humaneness. The Master said: “In your private hours be respectful, in your work be reverent, and with others be wholehearted. Even if you go to live among the tribes of the east and north, none of this may be let go.”
sentences.n: Three matching phrases, each a setting and then a quality. 居處 'dwelling and abiding', one's ordinary time at home (處 chǔ); 執事 'holding to one's business'; 與 yǔ 'with'. 之 is the verb 'to go to'; 雖 'even if'. Zhu Xi: 恭 governs the bearing, 敬 governs the business in hand; 恭 shows outwardly, 敬 rules within; 'cannot be cast aside even among the Yi and Di' urges him to hold them fast and not lose them. He quotes Master Cheng: this saying runs from top to bottom, and the sage never had two kinds of saying — fill it out and it shows in the glow of face and back (睟面盎背, from Mencius); carry it through and 'by earnest respect the world is set at peace' (篤恭而天下平, from the Doctrine of the Mean). And Hu Yin: Fan Chi asked about humaneness three times; this was the first, 'the hard part first' (6.20) next, and 'loving others' (12.22) probably last. Bao Xian (in He Yan): even going to the Yi and Di, where there are no rites and no right, one may still not cast these aside and fail to practise them.

sentences.t:
子貢問曰：「
何如斯可謂之士矣？」
子曰：「
行己有恥，
使於四方，
不辱君命：
可謂士矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
a region, a quarter, a direction

sentences.l:
Zigong asked, saying: “Being how, can one then be called an officer?”
The Master said: “Conducting himself with a sense of shame;
sent on missions to the four quarters,
not disgracing his lord's charge —
he can be called an officer.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked what it takes to be called an officer. The Master said: “One who, knowing shame, has things he will not stoop to, and who, sent abroad on his lord's business wherever it may be, brings no discredit on the charge he carries — he may be called an officer.”
sentences.n: The print has 已, a misprint for 己, corrected here. 行己 'to conduct oneself' needs 己 jǐ 'oneself' (as 5.15 其行己也恭); Ruan's 1816 text reads 己, and He Yan's print has 巳, its form for both graphs — the same confusion as at 4.14 and 5.15. 子貢 Zigong is the disciple Duanmu Ci 端木賜 (1.10). 何如斯可謂之士矣 is the frame of 12.20: 'being how, then can (one) be called an officer?' 士 'an officer, a man of service'. 行 xíng 'to conduct'. 使 'to go as envoy' — Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (shì, the envoy's reading, as at 6.3); modern practice reads shǐ, which we give. 四方 'the four quarters', in every direction. 辱 'to disgrace'; 君命 'the lord's charge'. Zhu Xi: this is the man whose will has things it will not do and whose talent is enough to do things; Zigong was a fine speaker, so he was told about missions — for the envoy's task is hard, and asks more than skill in speech. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): 'having shame' is having things one will not do (有恥有所不為).

sentences.t:
曰：「敢問其次。」
曰：「
宗族稱孝焉，
郷黨稱弟焉。」
sentences.i: “May I ask about the next grade?” “One whose kinsmen call him a good son, and whose neighbours call him a dutiful younger brother.”
sentences.n: 敢問 'may I venture to ask'. 其次 'the next (below it)': 次 is 'next in order'. 宗族 'lineage and clan', his kinsmen; 郷黨 'district and village', his neighbours (郷 is the edition's other form of 鄉, which it also prints; 鄉黨 as at 6.3 and 10.1). 稱 chēng 'to speak of, to praise as'. 焉 'in him, for it'. 弟 is tì 'deference to elders', a younger brother's virtue (Zhu Xi: 去聲 — the tì reading, against dì 'younger brother'). Zhu Xi: this is the man whose root is established but whose talent falls short, and so he comes next.

sentences.t:
曰：「敢問其次。」
曰：「
言必信，
行必果，
硜硜然小人哉！
抑亦可以為次矣。」
sentences.l:
He said: “May I venture to ask about the next?”
He said: “His words sure to be kept,
his conduct sure to be carried through —
clinking hard like pebbles, a small man indeed!
But he too can count as the next.”
sentences.i: “And the next?” “A man who always keeps his word and always sees through what he has begun: hard and narrow as a little stone, a man of small reach! Yet even he might be counted as the next grade.”
sentences.n: 言必信，行必果: two matching lines, 'his words — sure to be kept; his conduct — sure to be carried through' (信 good faith, being true to one's word). 行 is 'conduct' — Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (xìng, the noun); modern practice reads xíng. 果 'resolute, carrying through' (Zhu Xi: 果，必行也 'sure to act on it'; compare 6.6, of Zilu). 硜硜 kēng kēng (Zhu Xi: 苦耕反): Zhu Xi says 硜 is a small stone, hard and firm (小石之堅確者); 然 makes it a description. 小人 here is a man of shallow, narrow understanding (言其識量之淺狹), not the wicked man. 抑亦 'but still, even so'. Zhu Xi: in such a man neither root nor branch is worth looking at, but none of it spoils his keeping himself in hand, so the sage still allows him something; below this come the people of the market-place, who cannot be counted as officers at all. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 行必果 means whatever he means to do he dares to carry out; 硜硜 is the look of a small man. Variant: He Yan's text reads 硜硜然小人也 'a small man, that is what he is', with 也 for 哉.

sentences.t:
曰：「
今之従政者何如？」
子曰：「噫！
斗筲之人，
何足算也？」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
He said: “Those in government today — what of them?”
The Master said: “Hm!
Men of the peck and the basket —
how are they worth reckoning?”
sentences.i: “And what of those now in government?” The Master said: “Hm! Little men, the size of a grain-measure or a rice basket — why even count them?”
sentences.n: 従 is the edition's form of 從 cóng: 従政 'to follow the business of government', to hold office (6.6). 今之従政者 'those of today in government' — Zhu Xi: men such as the three houses of Lu. 噫 yī is here a sound of displeasure (Zhu Xi: 心不平聲; Zheng Xuan in He Yan the same), not the grief of 11.8. 斗 dǒu is a measure holding ten sheng; 筲 shāo (Zhu Xi: 所交反) a bamboo vessel holding a peck and two sheng: 斗筲之人 'men of a peck or a basket' means men mean and small (鄙細). 算 suàn 'to count, reckon' (Zhu Xi: 悉亂反; another text writes 筭; 算，數也). 何足 'how is it enough to', 'how are they worth'. Zhu Xi: each of Zigong's questions went lower than the last, so the Master warned him this way. He quotes Master Cheng: Zigong probably meant to do some bright, striking deed that would make him known; everything the Master told him was solid, earnest, and found within oneself.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不得中行而與之，
必也狂狷乎！
狂者進取，
狷者有所不為也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not getting those of the middle way to give it to,
if it must be anyone, it would be the wild and the guarded!
The wild press forward and take hold;
the guarded have things they will not do.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If I cannot find men who walk the middle way to pass it on to, I must make do with those who go too far and those who hold back. The first push ahead and seize on the good; the second have things they will not stoop to.”
sentences.n: 中行 'the middle way' — Zhu Xi: 行 is 'way' (行，道也), and he speaks of 'men of the middle way' (中道之人); He Yan's Bao Xian takes 行 as conduct: 'those whose conduct hits the mean'. 與之 'to give (it) to them' — Zhu Xi explains that the sage wanted men of the middle way to teach. 必也…乎 'if it must be someone, surely…' (12.13). 狂 is the 'wild' of 5.21 and 8.16, aiming high; 狷 juàn (Zhu Xi: 音絹) is holding back, keeping oneself clean. 進取 'to press forward and take'; 有所不為 'have things they do not do'. Zhu Xi: the wild aim very high but their conduct does not cover it; the guarded fall short in understanding but have more than enough in holding to themselves; if the sage could not find men of the middle way and found only the merely careful and decent, they might never rouse themselves to do anything — better these, whose will and principles can be spurred and checked to bring them on to the Way; not that he meant them to stop there. He quotes Mencius: Confucius surely wanted men of the middle way, but could not count on finding them, so he thought of the next — men like Qin Zhang, Zeng Xi and Mu Pi were what he called wild, grand in their aims, always crying 'the men of old, the men of old!', yet their conduct, looked at, did not cover their words; failing them, he wanted men who would not stoop to anything unclean — these are the guarded, and they come next again. Bao Xian (in He Yan): the wild press forward to take the good Way, the guarded keep to their principle and do nothing; he wanted these two because men of the day mostly went forward and back by turns, and he valued their steadiness.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
南人有言曰：『
人而無恒，
不可以作巫醫。』
善夫！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Southern people have a saying:
‘A man who lacks constancy
cannot be made a shaman or a healer.’
Good, that!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “They have a saying in the south: ‘A man who cannot hold steady is not fit even to serve as shaman or healer.’ Well said!”
sentences.n: 南人 'people of the south' (Zhu Xi: men of the southern states; Kong Anguo in He Yan the same). 人而無恒 'a man, and yet without constancy': 而 joins subject and predicate as in 3.3 人而不仁. 恒 héng 'constancy, holding steady' (Zhu Xi: 胡登反; 恒，常久也), as in 7.25 有恒者. 作 'to act as, be made'. 巫 is a shaman, 醫 a healer. Zhu Xi: the shaman deals with ghosts and spirits, the healer is entrusted with life and death; so though these are humble callings, they above all cannot be done without constancy. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads it the other way: shamans and healers cannot cure a man without constancy. 善夫 'good, that!': 夫 fú closes the exclamation (Zhu Xi: 音扶) — Zhu Xi and Bao Xian: the Master praises the southerners' saying. The Master's speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
不恒其徳，
或承之羞。
sentences.l:
Not constant in his virtue,
someone brings him shame.
sentences.i: If a man's virtue does not hold steady, someone will hand him disgrace.
sentences.n: The Master's speech continues, unquoted; the line he cites is given without marks, as the Ode lines of 12.10. Zhu Xi: these are the words on the third line (九三) of the hexagram 恒 'Constancy' in the Changes, and 承 is 'to bring forward, to present' (承，進也). 或 'someone, there will be one who'. 之 'him'. 羞 xiū 'shame, disgrace'. 徳 is the edition's form of 德. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): this is the text of the hexagram 恒; where virtue has no constancy, shame follows hard on it (羞厚承之).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不占而已矣。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Not divining — and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It is simply that they do not consult the omens.”
sentences.n: 占 zhān 'to divine, to read the omens'. 而已矣 'and that is all'. Zhu Xi: 子曰 is set down again to keep the Master's words apart from the text of the Changes; the meaning is not clear (其義未詳). He gives Yang Shi's reading, which he finds roughly workable: if the gentleman pondered the omens of the Changes he would know that inconstancy brings shame; men are inconstant simply because they do not consult them. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads it the other way round: the Changes are for divining good and ill fortune, and a man without constancy is one the Changes do not divine for — he is not worth the divining, and that is all.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子和而不同，
小人同而不和。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is at ease, and not the same;
the small man is the same, and not at ease.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman is easy with others but does not simply fall in with them; the small man falls in with others but is never easy with them.”
sentences.n: The two lines turn the same two words round, each joined by 而 'but'. 和 hé is 'ease' (1.12) — here, Zhu Xi says, a heart with nothing contrary or perverse in it (和者無乖戾之心); 同 'the same, at one with' is here the wish to fawn and side with others (同者有阿比之意). Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: the gentleman values what is right, so there are things on which he does not go along; the small man values profit — how could he be at ease with others? He Yan's own comment: the gentleman's heart is at ease, but what each sees differs, hence 'not the same'; small men like the same things, but each fights for his own profit, hence 'not at ease'.

sentences.t:
子貢問曰：「鄉人皆好之，何如？」
子曰：「未可也。」「鄉人皆惡之，何如？」
子曰：「未可也。
不如鄉人之善者好之，
其不善者惡之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Zigong asked, saying: “The people of his district all like him — what of that?”
The Master said: “Not yet enough.” “The people of his district all hate him — what of that?”
The Master said: “Not yet enough.
It is not as good as: the good ones of the district's people liking him,
their not-good ones hating him.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked: “What would you say of a man whom everyone in his district likes?” The Master said: “One cannot tell from that.” “And one whom everyone in his district hates?” “Nor from that. Better that the good among his neighbours should like him and the bad among them hate him.”
sentences.n: 鄉人 'the people of the district' (鄉 xiāng; as 10.10). 好 hào 'to like', 惡 wù 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 好惡並去聲). 未可也 'not yet acceptable' — not enough to judge him by. 不如 'is not as good as', and so 'better that…'. 其不善者 'the not-good ones among them': 其 points back to the district's people. Zhu Xi: the people of one district ought to hold a fair common view, yet even among them each likes and dislikes by his own kind; if the good like a man and the bad do not hate him, he must be one who goes along with anybody; if the bad hate him and the good do not like him, there must be nothing in him worth liking. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): good men think well of him and bad men hate him; so his approval of the good is plain and his hatred of the bad shown up (善善明悪悪著). Variant: He Yan's text ends 其不善者悪之也, with a closing 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子易事而難説也。
説之不以道，不説也；
及其使人也，器之。
小人難事而易説也。
説之雖不以道，説也；
及其使人也，求備焉。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman is easy to work for and hard to please. Try to please him by means that are not the Way, and he will not be pleased; and when he sets people to work, he takes each for what he is fit for. The small man is hard to work for and easy to please. Try to please him by means that are not the Way, and he will be pleased all the same; and when he sets people to work, he expects every one of them to be good at everything.”
sentences.n: Two halves built alike, with the terms reversed. 易 yì 'easy' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), 難 nán 'hard'; 説 yuè (Zhu Xi: 音悦) is both 'to please' with an object (説之 'pleasing him') and 'to be pleased' without one (不説). 易事 'easy to serve', 難説 'hard to please': the adjective comes first, the verb after it is taken passively. 以道 'by the Way', by right means. 及其…也 'when it comes to his…'. 器之 'treats them as vessels' — Zhu Xi: uses each according to his talent and capacity (隨其材器而使之), as each vessel serves its own use (2.12). 求備 'to seek completeness', expecting each man to be good at all things; 焉 'in them'. Zhu Xi: the gentleman's heart is public-minded and forbearing, the small man's private and harsh; between Heaven's principle and human desire it is always one way or the other. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): not demanding everything of one man, he is easy to serve; 器之 is weighing a man's talent and giving him office. Variant: He Yan's text reads 及其使人也器也 'he treats them as vessels', with 也 for 之.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子泰而不驕，
小人驕而不泰。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is assured and not haughty;
the small man is haughty and not assured.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman carries himself with quiet assurance but never with pride; the small man carries himself with pride but never with assurance.”
sentences.n: The two words are turned round, as in 13.23. 泰 tài 'great, grand' is here a bearing: Zhu Xi: the gentleman follows principle, so he is at peace and unhurried (安舒) and not puffed up or reckless (矜肆); the small man gives rein to his desires, so it is the reverse. In 9.3 the same word was 'arrogant', bigness taken too far. 驕 'haughty, proud'. He Yan's own comment: the gentleman is free and easy in himself, which can look like pride but is not; the small man is cramped and wary, yet in truth proud and self-satisfied.

sentences.t: 子曰：「剛、毅、木、訥，近仁。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Firm, resolute, plain, slow of speech — near to humaneness.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hard, steady, unpolished and slow to speak — such a man is not far from humaneness.”
sentences.n: Four single words, each a quality, then the verdict. 剛 'firm, unbending' (5.10); 毅 'resolute, enduring' (8.7); 木 'wood', here 'plain, unworked'; 訥 nè 'slow of speech' (4.24). Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: 木 is plain and simple (質樸), 訥 slow and halting (遲鈍); the four are qualities of the natural stuff that come near humaneness. And Yang Shi: firm and resolute, a man does not bend to the desires things rouse; plain and slow of speech, he does not run outward after things — so he is near humaneness. He Yan's Wang Su: 剛 is having no desires, 毅 daring and decisive, 木 plain and simple, 訥 slow and halting (遲鈍); one who has these four is close to humaneness. Compare 1.3: clever words and a pleasing face — 'rare indeed, humaneness'.

sentences.t:
子路問曰：「
何如斯可謂之士矣？」
子曰：「
切切偲偲，怡怡如也：
可謂士矣。
朋友切切偲偲，
兄弟怡怡。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
glad, at ease (only in 怡怡, Zhu Xi: 怡怡和悅也)
glad, at ease (only in 怡怡, Zhu Xi: 怡怡和悅也)
deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)
glad, at ease (only in 怡怡, Zhu Xi: 怡怡和悅也)
glad, at ease (only in 怡怡, Zhu Xi: 怡怡和悅也)

sentences.l:
Zilu asked, saying: “Being how, can one then be called an officer?”
The Master said: “Earnestly pressing, patiently urging, at ease and glad he is —
he can be called an officer.
With friends, earnestly pressing, patiently urging;
with brothers, at ease and glad.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked what it takes to be called an officer. The Master said: “A man who presses hard and urges patiently, and is at ease and glad in his manner, may be called an officer: pressing and urging with his friends, at ease and glad with his brothers.”
sentences.n: Zilu asks Zigong's question of 13.20 in the same words. Three reduplicated words, each doubling one graph for a manner; 如也 'the look of' closes the last, as in Book 10. 切 is read qiè here, not qiē 'to cut'; 偲 sī. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: 切切 is earnest and thorough (懇到), 偲偲 detailed in urging (詳勉), 怡怡 at ease and glad (和悦, as 10.4); all three were what Zilu lacked, so he was told them; and lest he muddle where each belongs — bringing on brothers the disaster of wounded kinship, and on friends the harm of mere softness (善柔) — the Master then set them apart. He Yan's Ma Rong: 切切偲偲 is the look of pressing and reproving one another, 怡怡 the look of easy agreement. Variant: He Yan's text ends 兄弟怡怡如也, repeating 如也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
善人教民七年，
亦可以即戎矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A good man teaching the people seven years —
they too can go to war.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Once a good man has been teaching the people for seven years, they are fit to be sent to war as well.”
sentences.n: 善人 'a good man' (7.25, 11.19). 教 jiào 'to teach' (the edition prints 教 here and in 13.30, 敎 elsewhere). 即 jí 'to go to, approach' (Zhu Xi: 即，就也); 戎 róng 'arms, war' (戎，兵也). 亦 'also, even'. Zhu Xi: teaching the people means teaching them the conduct of filial devotion, deference, wholeheartedness and good faith, and the ways of farming and of drill; the people then know to hold their superiors dear and die for their leaders, and so can go to war. He quotes Master Cheng: 'seven years' is the sage's measure of the time needed, like 'a full year' and 'three years' (13.10), 'a hundred years' (13.11), 'a generation' (13.12), and Mencius's 'a great state in five years, a small one in seven'; one should think out what is to be done in that time, and then it is of use. Bao Xian (in He Yan): 即戎 is to go to arms — they can attack and fight.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
以不教民戰，
是謂棄之。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Using untaught people to fight —
this is called casting them off.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Leading people into battle who have never been taught — that is what is meant by casting them away.”
sentences.n: 以 is here a verb, 'to use' (Zhu Xi: 以，用也). 不教民 'untaught people': 不教 describes 民. 是謂 'this is called' (2.7). Zhu Xi: to use untaught people in war is sure to bring the disaster of defeat and ruin — that is throwing away one's people. Ma Rong (in He Yan): to send people not drilled into battle is sure to end in rout; that is throwing them away. With this the book ends.
